# Grounded generator pilot -- AIMS-F

**Section 4 of the grounded-generator brief. Measured, not asserted.** Generated by
`scripts/gen-grounded-items.mjs` against `ISO/IEC 42001:2023` and formatted by
`scripts/emit-pilot-report.mjs` from `PILOT-GROUNDED-AIMSF-2.json`. Nothing in the live bank was touched: this
was a dry run, and the artifact is what `--apply --from=` would insert item for item.

## What the numbers are

| | |
|---|---|
| model | `claude-opus-5` |
| items attempted | 40, allocated across the domains by `weight_pct` |
| items the writer produced | 40 |
| **survivors** | **22** |
| rejected by a code gate | 17 |
| rejected by the blind solver | 1 |
| undecided (solver could not run) | 0 |
| tasks mapped to passages | 34 of 35 |


Allocation is by domain weight rather than evenly over tasks, because that is the basis
`generate-mock-exam` assembles a form on. A pilot spread evenly would over-sample the
light domains and say nothing about the shape of a real form.

## Why items were rejected

A single item can fail more than one gate, so these do not sum to the rejection count.

| n | gate |
|---|---|
| 18 | options probe: a cue in the options alone |
| 9 | code: anchor-is-primary |
| 8 | code: modal-fidelity |
| 7 | code: reproduction |
| 4 | code: structure |
| 1 | solver: second defensible option |
| 1 | code: shared-distractor-phrase |
| 1 | code: near-duplicate |

**`solver COULD NOT RUN` is not a rejection and is never counted as one.** A step that
could not start is not a step that failed: folding it into the rejections would blame the
items for the transport, and folding it into the survivors would clear items nobody checked.

## The gates, and which of them is not a model

| gate | what it checks | model involved |
|---|---|---|
| `clause-exists` | every clause named is in the library, and is not a declared library gap | no |
| `verbatim` | `key_support` occurs **exactly** in the named passage | no |
| `modal-fidelity` | a `must` claim needs a `shall` anchor in a `shall` clause | no |
| `superseded-wording` | retired edition wording anywhere in the item | no |
| `structure` | cue guard, key-as-longest, odd-one-out by negation and by opening word | no |
| `near-duplicate` | share of the **shorter** stem's distinctive terms against live items on the same task | no |
| `shared-distractor-phrase` | a run of 4+ words every distractor carries and the key does not | no |
| `anchor-is-primary` | the key anchors in a **primary** passage of the task, not a supporting one | no |
| `reproduction` | at most a 9-word run shared with any source, in any **served** field | no |
| blind solver | is it solvable to the key from the passages, with no second defensible option | **yes, and it never sees the key** |
| options-only probe | could a candidate with no knowledge pick the key from the option shapes | **yes, and it sees only the options** |

The three gates below the line are new in this run, and each answers a defect the director
found by reading the first pilot:

- **`anchor-is-primary`** takes out the off-task items. Two of the first pilot's survivors
  anchored in a real clause, verbatim, at the right modal strength -- and the clause was not
  what the task examines. Every gate that existed passed them.
- **`shared-distractor-phrase`** takes out the giveaway: three distractors ending in the same
  clause that the stem excludes.
- **`reproduction`** is the gap the first pilot had no gate for at all.

## The paraphrase retry

| | |
|---|---|
| reproduction failures given one retry | 13 |
| **fixed on retry** | **13** |
| still failing after retry | 0 |

The retry is offered for REPRODUCTION ONLY. It is the one failure a rewrite can fix without
changing what the item measures: the claim, the key and the anchor all stay and only our
wording moves. A modal error or a wrong anchor is a different item, so neither is retried.
The offending run is named in the retry -- "paraphrase this" without it rewrites around the
wrong span -- and the result is RE-GATED, never trusted.

## Reproduction in served fields

| | |
|---|---|
| ceiling, stem and options | a run of at most **9** words shared with any source |
| ceiling, explanation | 9 words unquoted, plus ONE attributed quotation of at most one sentence |
| longest served run, max across survivors | 9 |
| median | 7 |
| **survivors over the ceiling** | **0** |

The first pilot had no such gate and **17 of its 31 survivors carried a run of 10 words or
more**, the worst 20. The generator reproduces the standard because it is handed the
standard, which is the cost of grounding and the reason this gate is not optional here.

The runs are measured with the lesson scanner's own tokenisation -- one implementation. The
quotation allowance is a MODE in that module, not a copy. `key_support` is exempt because it
is never served.

**And the index is wider than the library.** The scanner holds nine documents, including
ISO/IEC 22989, 27000, 27004 and 27005, which the task map does not use. One rejection in this
run is a 16-word run against **22989:2022** -- a standard no passage was supplied from, so the
item reproduced it from recall while writing about something else. Scoring against the wider
index is deliberate: the ceiling is about what a candidate can recognise, and recognition does
not care which document we happened to map.

## Anchor clusters -- flagged, not rejected

Items in **different tasks** whose keys rest on the **same clause**. A candidate who reads
one learns the answer to the others, and stem identity cannot see it -- their stems differ,
which is exactly why the deployed dedupe misses them.

| clause | survivors | tasks |
|---|---|---|
| 4.1 | 2 | 1.2, 2.1 |
| 6.1.4 | 2 | 2.6, 2.7 |
| 7.2 | 2 | 3.1, 3.7 |

Recorded per item as `grounding_family`. **`generate-mock-exam` is not touched**, by
instruction; migration 376 adds the column so the assembler can dedupe on it if you rule that way.

## The options-only probe

A third model call on the survivors, seeing the four option texts and **nothing else** -- no
stem, no passages, no key. It flags an item a candidate with zero knowledge could answer from
the shape of the options. It never rejects: with four options it is right one time in four by
luck, so a flag needs both the key AND a concrete, checkable cue.

| | |
|---|---|
| survivors probed | 22 |
| **flagged** | **18** |
| probe could not run | 0 |

> **THIS RATE IS A DESIGN ERROR IN THE REPORT, NOT 18 FINDINGS.** 82 percent of survivors
> flagged. This repository's own rule is that a guard firing on the normal case gets deleted
> by the first person it inconveniences, and that a firing count above a stated threshold is
> a design error rather than a backlog of fixes. So the members were read before the number
> was reported.

> **AND READING THEM FOUND ONE PATTERN, NOT 18.** 12 of the 18 cues describe the same thing:
> the generator makes a distractor wrong by ADDING AN ABSOLUTE OR RESTRICTIVE QUALIFIER, or a
> self-justifying "because..." clause, and leaves the key as the plain statement. That is one
> habit of the writer prompt, and it is exploitable without knowing the subject.

> **The remedy is the one you ruled: rewrite the cue out.** Not a harder gate, not trickery,
> not a longer stem. It belongs in the writer prompt -- tell it not to manufacture a wrong
> answer by qualifying a right one -- and that is a change to what the generator ACCEPTS, so
> it is not made here. The remaining 6 cues are parallelism and length, listed below.

## Survivors

Each shows the anchor the item points at. **`key_support` is internal**: it is a sentence
copied out of a licensed standard as the evidence that the item is supported, and it is
never shown to a candidate, returned by a function, or served through MCP.

### 1. AIMS-F · D1 · task 1.2

**A company develops an AI model in house, deploys it in its own operations, and also sells access to it as a hosted service. Its AI management system team has just worked through the context clause and identified where the organization sits relative to that AI system. Which statement about this role determination is correct?**

- **`KEY` a) The roles identified can shape which requirements and controls apply, and to what extent.**
- b) The organization has to settle on one single role, because only one role can apply to any given AI system at a time.
- c) Identifying the organization's roles is offered purely as advice, so an organization may skip it and still conform.
- d) Testers and evaluators, as well as deployers, are listed as top-level role categories that sit entirely outside the AI producer category.

*explanation:* Under clause 4.1, where an organization sits relative to an AI system can govern which obligations and Annex A measures bite, and how far they bite, so role identification feeds directly into applicability decisions.

*`key_support` — ISO/IEC 42001 clause 4.1:*

> The organization’s roles can determine the applicability and extent of applicability of the requirements and controls in this document.

*blind solver:* answered A, no second defensible option — Clause 4.1 states "The organization's roles can determine the applicability and extent of applicability of the requirements and controls in this document."

*gates:* clause-exists pass (4) · verbatim pass (4) · modal-fidelity pass (1) · superseded-wording pass (6) · structure pass (4) · near-duplicate pass (18) · shared-distractor-phrase pass (3) · anchor-is-primary pass (1) · reproduction pass (6)

*longest served run:* 5 words in the explanation  (ceiling 9)   *anchor family:* 4.1   **OPTIONS-PROBE FLAG (only-hedged)**

### 2. AIMS-F · D1 · task 1.4

**Annex D of ISO/IEC 42001 discusses operating the AI management system alongside other management system standards. According to Annex D, what makes combined use with ISO/IEC 27001 easier for an organization?**

- **`KEY` a) Both ISO/IEC 27001 and the AI management system use the high-level structure.**
- b) ISO/IEC 27001 is the normative reference whose content forms requirements of ISO/IEC 42001.
- c) ISO/IEC 27701 certification has to be obtained first so that privacy controls can be mapped across.
- d) Conformity to ISO 9001 substitutes for the AI management system's own risk management planning.

*explanation:* The ISO/IEC 27001 bullet in Annex D.2 explains that because the two standards share the same harmonised clause architecture, running them together is made easier and brings the organization considerable advantage.

*`key_support` — ISO/IEC 42001 clause D.2:*

> Given that both ISO/IEC 27001 and the AI management systems use the high-level structure, their integrated use is facilitated and of great benefit for the organization.

*blind solver:* answered A, no second defensible option — Clause D.2 states "Given that both ISO/IEC 27001 and the AI management systems use the high-level structure, their integrated use is facilitated and of great benefit for the organization."

*gates:* clause-exists pass (4) · verbatim pass (4) · modal-fidelity pass (1) · superseded-wording pass (6) · structure pass (4) · near-duplicate pass (17) · shared-distractor-phrase pass (3) · anchor-is-primary pass (2) · reproduction pass (6)

*longest served run:* 8 words in the option a  (ceiling 9)   *anchor family:* D.2   **OPTIONS-PROBE FLAG (odd-verdict)**

### 3. AIMS-F · D2 · task 2.1

**A retailer already maintains an ISO/IEC 27001 context analysis (regulators, customers, suppliers, threat landscape) and is now extending it to cover an AI recommendation system. Which determination does the AIMS context clause oblige the retailer to make in addition to its existing security-shaped analysis?**

- **`KEY` a) Determine whether climate change is a relevant issue for the organization.**
- b) Determine and document its obligations to report information about the AI system to interested parties.
- c) Determine an F1 value that the recommendation model is expected to meet in production.
- d) Determine that confidentiality, integrity and availability of data are the only AI-related concerns needing treatment.

*explanation:* Clause 4.1 states an explicit obligation to decide whether climate change is a relevant issue, alongside determining external/internal issues, the intended purpose of the AI systems and the organization's roles.

*`key_support` — ISO/IEC 42001 clause 4.1:*

> The organization shall determine whether climate change is a relevant issue.

*blind solver:* answered A, no second defensible option — Clause 4.1 explicitly states "The organization shall determine whether climate change is a relevant issue" as part of understanding the organization and its context, alongside intended purpose and role determination.

*gates:* clause-exists pass (4) · verbatim pass (4) · modal-fidelity pass (1) · superseded-wording pass (6) · structure pass (4) · near-duplicate pass (18) · shared-distractor-phrase pass (3) · anchor-is-primary pass (2) · reproduction pass (6)

*longest served run:* 8 words in the option a  (ceiling 9)   *anchor family:* 4.1

### 4. AIMS-F · D2 · task 2.2

**A retailer develops one in-house demand-forecasting model, uses a purchased CRM whose vendor has switched on an embedded lead-scoring feature, and has support staff calling a third-party large language model API. The AI programme lead proposes an AIMS scope reading "AI systems developed by us", arguing the other two are somebody else's products. Applying Clause 4.3, what is the most defensible way to settle the boundary?**

- a) Leave the scope as an internal management decision recorded only in meeting minutes, since documented information is retained for the risk treatment process rather than for the boundary.
- b) Keep the "developed by us" boundary and justify leaving the CRM feature and the LLM API out by recording them as excluded controls in the statement of applicability, with reasons for exclusion.
- **`KEY` c) Bring the embedded CRM feature and the LLM API inside the boundary, deciding applicability from the 4.1 issues and 4.2 interested-party requirements, and keep the scope as documented information.**
- d) Restrict the scope to the forecasting model, because the context clause only asks the organization to consider the intended purpose of AI systems it develops itself, and the vendor retains the remaining obligations.

*explanation:* Clause 4.3 requires the organization to determine boundaries and applicability by considering the 4.1 external/internal issues and the 4.2 interested-party requirements, and the resulting scope shall be available as documented information. Clause 4.1 expressly covers AI systems developed, provided or used, so vendor-embedded and API-based AI in use is within the field of consideration; the boundary cannot be narrowed to self-built systems by assertion.

*`key_support` — ISO/IEC 42001 clause 4.3:*

> When determining this scope, the organization shall consider: — the external and internal issues referred to in 4.1; — the requirements referred to in 4.2.

*blind solver:* answered C, no second defensible option — Clause 4.3 requires the scope to be determined from the 4.1 internal/external issues and 4.2 interested-party requirements and to be available as documented information, and 4.1 expressly covers AI systems "developed, provided or used by the organization", so the vendor-embedded CRM feature and the third-party LLM API cannot be excluded merely because someone else built them.

*gates:* clause-exists pass (4) · verbatim pass (4) · modal-fidelity pass (1) · superseded-wording pass (6) · structure pass (4) · near-duplicate pass (18) · shared-distractor-phrase pass (3) · anchor-is-primary pass (1) · reproduction pass (6)

*longest served run:* 7 words in the explanation  (ceiling 9)   *anchor family:* 4.3   **OPTIONS-PROBE FLAG (odd-verdict)**

### 5. AIMS-F · D2 · task 2.4

**Top management of an AI provider has signed an assignment matrix naming owners for risk management, data quality, security, privacy and AI system impact assessment, and has named a manager accountable for ensuring the AI management system conforms to the standard. The matrix is circulated to all staff. Reviewing this against the leadership requirements, what gap remains?**

- **`KEY` a) No one holds the authority to report on how the AIMS is performing to top management.**
- b) Owners have not been named for every area listed in the guidance, such as human oversight and supplier relationships, which the standard requires in all cases.
- c) The assignments were not made by the governing body, which alone may allocate AIMS responsibilities and authorities.
- d) There is no gap; naming an owner for impact assessment and for conformity of the AI management system satisfies the leadership requirements.

*explanation:* Clause 5.3 lists two specific assignments top management shall make: authority for ensuring conformity of the AIMS, and authority for reporting AIMS performance to top management. Only the first has been assigned, so the reporting authority is unowned.

*`key_support` — ISO/IEC 42001 clause 5.3:*

> Top management shall assign the responsibility and authority for: a) ensuring that the AI management system conforms to the requirements of this document; b) reporting on the performance of the AI management system to top management.

*blind solver:* answered A, no second defensible option — Clause 5.3 requires top management to assign responsibility and authority both for (a) conformance of the AI management system and (b) reporting on AIMS performance to top management, and only the conformance role has been assigned.

*gates:* clause-exists pass (4) · verbatim pass (4) · modal-fidelity pass (1) · superseded-wording pass (6) · structure pass (4) · near-duplicate pass (18) · shared-distractor-phrase pass (3) · anchor-is-primary pass (2) · reproduction pass (6)

*longest served run:* 7 words in the stem  (ceiling 9)   *anchor family:* 5.3

### 6. AIMS-F · D2 · task 2.5

**A fintech firm is running its first AI risk assessment for a credit-scoring model. The analysis step records, for each identified risk, the potential financial and reputational loss to the firm, the realistic likelihood where it can be estimated, and the resulting risk level. An internal reviewer flags the analysis as incomplete against the AI risk assessment process requirements. Which correction addresses the gap?**

- **`KEY` a) Broaden the consequence analysis to also cover effects on individuals and societies, not only on the firm.**
- b) Assign a realistic likelihood value to every identified risk, with no exceptions permitted.
- c) Determine, during the analysis step, all Annex A controls needed and check that none have been omitted.
- d) Derive the risk criteria from the risk levels once they have been determined for all identified risks.

*explanation:* Clause 6.1.2 d) 1) requires the analysis of AI risks to assess potential consequences to the organization, individuals and societies. The firm assessed only consequences to itself, so the consequence scope must be widened.

*`key_support` — ISO/IEC 42001 clause 6.1.2:*

> assess the potential consequences to the organization, individuals and societies that would result if the identified risks were to materialize

*blind solver:* answered A, no second defensible option — Clause 6.1.2 d) 1) requires the analysis to assess potential consequences to the organization, individuals and societies, so limiting it to firm-level financial/reputational loss is the gap.

*gates:* clause-exists pass (4) · verbatim pass (4) · modal-fidelity pass (1) · superseded-wording pass (6) · structure pass (4) · near-duplicate pass (18) · shared-distractor-phrase pass (3) · anchor-is-primary pass (2) · reproduction pass (6)

*longest served run:* 8 words in the explanation  (ceiling 9)   *anchor family:* 6.1.2   **OPTIONS-PROBE FLAG (shared-phrase)**

### 7. AIMS-F · D2 · task 2.6

**A deployment team has completed an AI system impact assessment for a customer-service chatbot. The assessment covers only the benefits and consequences of the system's intended use, and the results have been documented. Applying Clause 6.1.4, which action does the organization need to take next?**

- **`KEY` a) Extend the assessment to the consequences of reasonably foreseeable misuse of the system.**
- b) Delay documenting the assessment results until a regulator or customer formally requests them.
- c) Publish the assessment results to every interested party before the chatbot is released.
- d) Keep the assessment results separate from the risk assessment so that the two processes stay independent.

*explanation:* Clause 6.1.4 requires the impact assessment to determine potential consequences of deployment, intended use AND foreseeable misuse; an assessment limited to intended use is incomplete. The other options contradict the documentation requirement, the conditional ('where appropriate', 'can') provision on making results available, and the requirement to consider the results in the risk assessment.

*`key_support` — ISO/IEC 42001 clause 6.1.4:*

> The AI system impact assessment shall determine the potential consequences an AI system’s deployment, intended use and foreseeable misuse has on individuals or groups of individuals, or both, and societies.

*blind solver:* answered A, no second defensible option — Clause 6.1.4 requires the impact assessment to determine consequences of the AI system's deployment, intended use and foreseeable misuse, so an assessment covering only intended use must be extended to reasonably foreseeable misuse.

*gates:* clause-exists pass (4) · verbatim pass (4) · modal-fidelity pass (1) · superseded-wording pass (6) · structure pass (4) · near-duplicate pass (18) · shared-distractor-phrase pass (3) · anchor-is-primary pass (6) · reproduction pass (6)

*longest served run:* 6 words in the explanation  (ceiling 9)   *anchor family:* 6.1.4   **OPTIONS-PROBE FLAG (odd-verdict)**

### 8. AIMS-F · D2 · task 2.7

**A deployment team has completed an AI risk assessment for a new recruitment-screening model. The analysis assessed consequences to the organization, to individuals and to societies, determined risk levels, and prioritised risks for treatment. On that basis the team proposes to close out the AI system impact assessment as "already covered", noting that no results will be shared outside the organization. How should this proposal be evaluated?**

- **`KEY` a) It is unsound: the impact assessment, anchored in deployment, intended use and foreseeable misuse, is separately needed and its results feed the risk assessment.**
- b) It is acceptable, because the risk analysis has already assessed potential consequences to individuals and societies, which is exactly the ground the impact assessment covers.
- c) It is acceptable only if the reverse is done instead, that is, the impact assessment is performed and the risk assessment closed out, since the impact assessment documents consequences in greater technical and societal detail.
- d) It is acceptable in this case, because the impact assessment becomes necessary only where the organization intends to make its results available to regulators, customers or other interested parties.

*explanation:* Clause 6.1.4 establishes the AI system impact assessment as a distinct requirement anchored in the AI system's deployment, intended use and foreseeable misuse, with a documented result, and expressly directs that its results be considered in the risk assessment of 6.1.2. It is therefore an input to, not a duplicate of, the risk assessment, and the risk assessment cannot discharge it.

*`key_support` — ISO/IEC 42001 clause 6.1.4:*

> The organization shall consider the results of the AI system impact assessment in the risk assessment (see 6.1.2).

*blind solver:* answered A, no second defensible option — Clause 6.1.4 mandates a defined AI system impact assessment process addressing deployment, intended use and foreseeable misuse, documented and whose results 'shall' be considered in the 6.1.2 risk assessment, and 8.4 requires it be performed at planned intervals — so it cannot be absorbed into the risk assessment.

*gates:* clause-exists pass (4) · verbatim pass (4) · modal-fidelity pass (1) · superseded-wording pass (6) · structure pass (4) · near-duplicate pass (18) · shared-distractor-phrase pass (3) · anchor-is-primary pass (2) · reproduction pass (6)

*longest served run:* 8 words in the explanation  (ceiling 9)   *anchor family:* 6.1.4   **OPTIONS-PROBE FLAG (odd-verdict)**

### 9. AIMS-F · D3 · task 3.1

**A deployer's AI team is made up entirely of machine-learning engineers with strong modelling and data-science backgrounds. A review of the system's high-risk use case shows that nobody on the team has education, training or experience in human oversight of AI decisions, and this gap affects AI performance. Applying the competence requirements, what is the organization's next step?**

- **`KEY` a) Act to acquire the missing competence, then evaluate whether the action taken was effective.**
- b) Deliver an awareness briefing to all team members on the AI policy and the implications of non-conformity, which covers the gap.
- c) Identify and document the resources required at each AI system life cycle stage, which discharges the competence obligation.
- d) Redraw the boundaries and applicability of the AI management system so that the human oversight activity falls outside the declared scope.

*explanation:* Clause 7.2 requires the organization, where applicable, to take actions to acquire the necessary competence and to evaluate the effectiveness of those actions (e.g. training, mentoring, reassignment, hiring or contracting), with documented information available as evidence of competence.

*`key_support` — ISO/IEC 42001 clause 7.2:*

> where applicable, take actions to acquire the necessary competence, and evaluate the effectiveness of the actions taken

*blind solver:* answered A, no second defensible option — Clause 7.2 requires that, where applicable, the organization 'take actions to acquire the necessary competence, and evaluate the effectiveness of the actions taken' (e.g. training, mentoring, hiring), which is exactly the identified gap affecting AI performance.

*gates:* clause-exists pass (4) · verbatim pass (4) · modal-fidelity pass (1) · superseded-wording pass (6) · structure pass (4) · near-duplicate pass (18) · shared-distractor-phrase pass (3) · anchor-is-primary pass (2) · reproduction pass (6)

*longest served run:* 9 words in the option d  (ceiling 9)   *anchor family:* 7.2   **OPTIONS-PROBE FLAG (shared-phrase)**

### 10. AIMS-F · D3 · task 3.3

**An AI governance team has drafted a new internal procedure for bias testing and intends to issue it as part of the AIMS. Before the procedure is released for use, which action does the AIMS documented information requirement place on the organization?**

- a) Have top management approve the draft during its planned review of the AI management system.
- b) Identify the draft as external-origin documented information and bring it under control on that basis.
- **`KEY` c) Review and approve the draft for suitability and adequacy, with appropriate identification, format and media.**
- d) Determine and document the organization's obligations to report the procedure's content to regulators and customers.

*explanation:* Clause 7.5.2 applies when documented information is created or updated: the organization shall ensure appropriate identification and description, format and media, and review and approval for suitability and adequacy. That is the applicable obligation before issuing the new procedure.

*`key_support` — ISO/IEC 42001 clause 7.5.2:*

> When creating and updating documented information, the organization shall ensure appropriate: — identification and description (e.g. a title, date, author or reference number); — format (e.g. language, software version, graphics) and media (e.g. paper, electronic); — review and approval for suitability and adequacy.

---

## What this pilot does not show

- **Tier A and Tier B rates are a HUMAN READ, and this report is not one.** The target was
  zero Tier A and a Tier B rate well under 9%. Nothing here can claim either: a Tier A
  finding is a wrong key, and the instrument that establishes a key is wrong is somebody
  reading the item against the standard. What the gates establish is narrower and worth
  saying exactly: every survivor points at a real sentence in a pinned edition, the
  sentence says what the item claims it says at the strength the item claims, and a model
  that never saw the key reached the key from the passages alone.
- **A DEFINITION CLAUSE'S `normative` CLASS IS THE WEAKEST THING IN THE LIBRARY.** The
  extractor classes a passage by the strongest modal in its own text, which is right for a
  requirement clause and crude for a terms-and-definitions entry: a definition whose note
  contains the word *can* is classed `can`, and a definition imposes nothing at all. One
  rejection in this run turns on that (clause 3.2). Refusing is still the right direction --
  an item may not say *should* on the authority of a definition -- but the class is a proxy
  and `informative` would describe those rows better.
- **The near-duplicate gate compares stems.** Two items with different stems and the same
  answer are invisible to it -- which is exactly the eight near-duplicate pairs the
  480-item audit found by reading. A threshold cannot find those.
- **A dry run of a generator is a sample, not a preview.** A second run writes different
  items. These are the items that were gated, because the artifact was persisted first.
- **The library is PARTIAL where it says so.** No item was refused for naming a missing clause in this run.

## The comparison the decision actually needs

This report cannot be read against the old generator on its own. The old path's error rate
is known from a human read -- 16 wrong keys in 822 items, 1.9% -- and the equivalent number
for these survivors requires the same instrument: somebody reading them against ISO/IEC
42001:2023. The survivors above are laid out in `AUDIT-SAMPLE.md`'s format so that read can
happen the same way, and each one carries the sentence it rests on so the reading is against
the standard's own words rather than against recall.
